title: Collapse, Renewal and the Struggle for Narrative Honesty
author: Phil Wilson
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/markus-spiske-
RN14PbITnnM-
unsplash-680x453.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/10/collapse-
renewal-and-the-struggle-for-narrative-honesty/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/markus-spiske-
RN14PbITnnM-unsplash-680x453.jpg)

Image by Markus Spiske.

I am in Port Orchard, Washington, with my wife, Shelly, staying at The Comfort
Inn all the way across The Generic States of America, where collective suicide
has been dressed in a happy face. Humanity, under the auspices of global
capitalism, tap dances its way to extinction. The end of the biosphere is
being televised on FOX News in the breakfast area to the accompaniment of
three varieties of glyphosate-infused cereal. Washington, the one-time
“Evergreen State,” is being reimagined as the “Smoldering Ash State” right on
FOX News. Wildfires rage in Spokane we learn with a graphic illustration of a
skeletal house photo, and not just Spokane but some place called Kaiser
Canyon, and somewhere else named Sinlahekin, and also in Modrite and throw in
The Cascade Range. It is FOX News so we don’t have clips of climate experts,
or even the bare mention of climate, at least I don’t hear it said while
absent-mindedly gazing out of the window across Puget Sound where the National
Anthem blares in brassy resonance from a Naval Base featuring battleships at
rest in calm, cold waters. Perhaps someone mutters the word climate as a
formal nod to the pretense of journalism. As a responsible caveat, I might
have missed it while spreading Jiff on white bread. Yes, vegan diets have low
points too.

We are in Port Orchard to celebrate the first birthday of our only grandchild,
Björn. I am obliged to perform a few cerebral-cortex backflips to avoid
thinking about the future being foretold in shadowy skies. It is a particular,
narrow tightrope that our grandchildren will cross, mottled with the empty
seduction of competition, the wrong turns of addiction and greed, and the
possibility/certainty of societal/environmental collapse. We are the
grandparents of armageddon, displaying a cell-phone video proudly to absolute
strangers at the hotel. Our grandson, a bright, smiling innocent child,
miraculously befriends a squirrel and pets her gently, and we have it on
video.

A flight across the nation uncovers a very simple revelation - the stars each
evening occupy the same sky in Northampton, Massachusetts and Port Orchard.
There is Venus, there is The Big Dipper, and a small matter of over 3K miles
on Jet Blue cannot change the frantic highways and generic institutions that
define every geographic point of our tedious nation. The same Denny’s, the
same McDonald’s, the same Taco Bell, the same Home Depot pass by like
telephone poles whizzing past a train car. The country has been tamed by
monstrous, unnatural forces that mock one’s sense of adventure. There is
natural beauty: Mt. Rainier across the Puget Sound, stands of Douglas Fir,
taller than our local hemlocks, and blackberries in ridiculous abundance. One
is left suspended between despair and wonder.

But the homogenized imprint, the sameness of a McDonald’s colonizing town
after town, in the fashion of a viral pandemic that duplicates itself
infinitely at the cost of the host, tells you that the organism we call planet
earth is churning agonizingly, mouth agape, spewing pieces of red spittle -
the flames raking Spokane. We don’t easily, the huddled, befuddled masses
yearning to breathe at all, connect MacDonald’s rapacious plundering of
Brazilian rain forest for burger grazing to the smoky skies delaying our
Flight at Sea-Tac Airport. And it is not enough for McDonald’s to merely burn
down the planet and coat our veins with hardened sludge, if we wander on to
their corporate web page we our whacked across the cranium with this:

> “The philosophy is to advocate for policies that we believe are relevant to
> our operations, can help improve the lives of our people and the communities
> where we operate, and also help protect the natural resources on which our
> System depends. Decisions are made at every level of government that can
> have a significant impact on our operating ecosystem. We believe it is
> important to understand key policy areas that impact our business and work
> with policy makers and other organizations to express our views.”

Every corporation has a “philosophy” and in Port Orchard, like everywhere else
in America, all the roads converge on Colonel Sanders, Taco Bell and Pizza Hut
- subsidiaries of the world’s biggest restaurant conglomerate (Yum Foods)
whose spin-masters tell us:

> “Everything we do ladders up to our [Recipe for Good
> Growth](https://www.yum.com/wps/portal/yumbrands/Yumbrands/company/about-
> yum-brands/good-growth-strategy) grounded in the idea that our growth and
> brand relevance will only endure if our brands are accessible, sustainable
> and reflective of evolving employee, franchisee and stakeholder needs.”

Even Chevron has ideals and a website for public bullshit:

> “Our purpose. Chevron’s purpose is to provide affordable, reliable, ever-
> cleaner energy. To enable human progress. That is at the heart of who we
> are.”

I am uncertain who is paid to create corporate slogans, and what sort of
gullible subjects consume them, but as I contemplate the smoky skies drifting
in from Spokane and look at the innocent eyes of my one-year-old grandson, I
am led down the path of speculation. We enter the second quarter of the 21st
century, with an unprecedented relationship to the future - we are on the cusp
of a moment that cannot maintain itself for long. I was born in a naive and
foolish time, an era of collective, self-congratulatory triumph - however
illusory. The great war was won and people procreated in a dull frenzy. The
path ahead opened broadly, brightly (so we thought) - no longer. The road
forks abruptly, tensely, shifting at a particularly opaque juncture.

Our personal longings, fears and dreams find expression in some of the best
leftist writing, for we all live precariously at the juncture where collapse
and (the hope of) renewal vie. Such brilliant writers as Balázs Matics and
Jeremy Lent give voice to each. I believe that all aging people find relief in
their approaching deaths, just under the wire of something stark, inevitable
and ferociously ominous in its leisurely but certain approach. But for our
children, grandchildren or for humanity in the abstract, one has to fight back
against the arsonists and psychopaths who embody capitalism’s lust for even a
pyric victory.

Balázs Matics, a Hungarian scholar, writes a blog entitled “[The Honest
Sorcerer](https://thehonestsorcerer.substack.com/),” that traces our dire
trajectory with such unflinching courage that one is utterly remiss to ignore
his political/environmental/cultural forecasts. His eyes are so far ahead of
the standard media that the only excuse for overlooking his work is that you
haven’t discovered him yet. That is no longer an option for my readers. [Here
is The Honest Sorcerer dispensing plain
truth](https://thehonestsorcerer.substack.com/p/civilizations-fall-when-this-
mechanism) in a new piece called, Civilizations Fall When This Mechanism
Activates:

> “Yet, instead of admitting that we’ve reached a dead-end and planning for
> the long descent ahead, the ruling strata of our civilization (not just in
> Europe but everywhere else, too) still keeps pretending that drilling more
> wells or building a few windmills and batteries could solve the issue… In
> the meantime great powers have merrily engaged in wars already over who
> controls the last remaining resources and trade routes on Earth. It
> increasingly looks like that some ‘elite’ circles have finally came to a
> conclusion: there is  _already_ not enough to go around. Well, by thinking
> and doing so they really make sure that there  _won’t be_ enough to go
> around—and that we will get there much sooner than it otherwise would have
> to be the case.”

Matics has a particular focus on the implacable/perseverative impulses
animating capitalism - the fetishization of technology in the face of
diminishing returns, as resources are both depleted and stacked on top of one
another in a desperate maneuver to increase growth and profits while the earth
stubbornly yields diminishing returns. Few writers provide a more graphic
critique of renewable energy which clearly does not constitute a new paradigm,
but continues the exhaustive and futile quest to drive production -
reflexively and unsustainably. Coal, gas and diesel drive the process of
renewable extraction, and renewables don’t replace fossil fuels, but are
simply stacked (in the fashion of geological strata) as impulsive,
undifferentiated means of subduing the planet.

Invoking historian Ronald Wright’s concept of “[Progress
Traps](https://reviewcanada.ca/magazine/2004/12/the-traps-of-progress/),”
Matics illustrates how the overconsumption and collapse of ancient
civilizations, beguiled by the illusion of limitless abundance, yet destroyed
by the exhaustion of precious resources succumbing to “overshoot,”
encapsulates the historical roots of collapsing modernity. The Honest Sorcerer
concludes his latest blog post with an optimistic, if vague thought:

> “We need a new paradigm built around [robustness, reciprocity and
> regeneration](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kzzr15cEg3o), giving back as
> much as possible to the living world on which our survival ultimately
> depends, so that it can take care of us and our descendants. Extracting one-
> time reserves of minerals (metal ores and fossil fuels alike), destroying
> the soil with industrial agriculture or polluting the atmosphere and rivers
> will not cut it. Only reciprocity can. Restoring biodiversity—even if its a
> small region you live in—or implementing the principles of agro-ecology,
> building low-tech but robust machines and tools from the scraps left behind
> by this civilization, and cooperating with neighbors is the only way
> through. I’m not suggesting that success is guaranteed, but doing more of
> the same will surely see us fail. Again.”

Unlike Matics,[ Jeremy Lent imagines a full throated triumph for justice and
equality emerging out of the worst impulse of
capitalism](https://jeremylent.substack.com/p/ai-and-ecocivilization-the-
unexpected) (in the second of a 3 pt. series entitled, AI and Ecocivilization:
The Unexpected Opportunity) - the creation and expansion of Artificial
Intelligence. Lent sees AI as a tool for extraction and exploitation, but, as
the ultimate act of “enclosure,” stealing all of humanity’s intellectual
property for profit, he envisions an unprecedented explosion of revolutionary
public fervor:

> “At this pivotal moment, we are now facing an enclosure of far greater
> scale. The large language models reshaping our economy were trained on the
> accumulated knowledge, creativity, and expressions of humanity—books, art,
> conversations, code, scientific discoveries, and cultural traditions built
> up over countless generations. These treasures represent the cumulative
> ingenuity and industriousness of our ancestors going back to earliest times:
> the commonwealth of our shared human legacy. Now, captured by a handful of
> corporations, this immeasurable inheritance is being repackaged as a
> proprietary product and sold back to us, while the value it generates is
> funneled up the wealth pump to a tiny elite.
>
> This is the result of what I’ve referred to as [Windigo’s
> Law](https://jeremylent.substack.com/p/our-civilizations-disease-has-a-
> name), operating now at unprecedented scale. But the very magnitude of this
> brazen theft opens up an opportunity. Once people recognize that AI is built
> on the theft of our commonwealth, an inescapable moral conclusion is that
> the wealth it generates rightly belongs, in significant part, to all of us.
> This calls for a massive response based on a foundation of collective moral
> outrage.”

I note that Lent departs from Matics on the matter of technology, seeing it as
an endeavor possessing moral worth determined by the forces that control it.
Lent goes on to conceptualize a future society in which AI is not only owned
as a common good, but uniquely “democratized” with a controlling political
structure comprised of ordinary citizens chosen via “Sortition” (random lot).

The publicly owned and equitably distributed spoils of AI would require the
uniquely democratic structure of Citizens’ Assemblies as a matter of
protection from future whims to assert enclosure. According to Lent:

“Its sortition structure would shield it from both corporate lobbying and
political pressure—and, unlike a conventional regulatory agency, it would
carry a direct mandate from the public it serves.”

But Lent stops short in this essay of broadening the idea of a publicly
controlled vision of AI to the more general issue of democracy and power.

He calls for mass participation:

> “The future is not a spectator sport: it is something we all co-create as
> part of the interconnected web of our collective thoughts, ideas, and
> actions” but does not imagine (in this particular piece) a system of
> governance in which all decision making resides within the body of the
> citizenry. Nor does he discuss the larger question of the purpose of AI
> beyond simply generating shared wealth. As it now stands, AI functions as a
> profit driven mechanism to inspire enormous investments with the prospect of
> replacing human labor with technology. But labor, human or robotic, under
> capitalism has been a tool for extraction, imperialism and war. If AI is not
> merely a means of profit (shared or hoarded) but a tool for human, animal
> and environmental well-being then it will need to be strictly regulated and
> limited in scope. AI is enormously polluting to the environment with huge
> expenditures of both water and fossil fuels. Perhaps, its only immediate use
> ought to be for the planning and implementation of the critical “[Degrowth
> Economy](https://www.jasonhickel.org/less-is-more)”

These issues are uniquely within Jeremy Lent’s “wheelhouse,” and I look
forward to his expanded thoughts on AI (as an aspect of a just society) in the
upcoming third part of his series.

Such an economy would require a radical transition from systems of enclosure
to wholesale expansion of “The Commons” – public transportation rather than
private vehicles, public swimming pools and exercise facilities rather than
privately owned equipment, local farming cooperatives rather than industrial
agriculture, and an overall shift from a philosophy of individual ambition to
mutual cooperation. Jeremy Lent has expanded on the subject of human
possibility and environmental harmony [with singular
depth](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s3R5ONzURns). He is a storyteller from
a world that has only been realized in brief, local instances, but now, Lent
argues, we must see past our habitual, limited horizons.

The dichotomy of “collapse and renewal” demands a profound narrative shift.
The biggest question to me involves the transition from capitalist
brainwashing to environmental class consciousness, a shift from pseudo-
electoral democracy to “Direct Democracy,” and, critically, mass access to the
narrative of collapse. As the collapse looms and accelerates, ordinary people
must have a coherent story that describes our collective predicament. [This
TED Talk by Bill McKibben](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9LTGzEzDat0)
illustrates how even the most respected voices in the “environmental movement”
have been coopted by capital (most likely, unknowingly - I do not question
McKibben’s idealistic intentions). McKibben’s talk makes it seem like the
renewable energy industry is poised to save us – all we have to do is follow
the market trends making solar cheaper than coal. That is not, as The Honest
Sorcerer instructs us, how capitalism operates. Bill McKibben and The Honest
Sorcerer are quietly locked in a narrative struggle to create a story able to
mobilize the working class. Sadly, McKibben has a larger platform than Balázs
Matics (The Honest Sorcerer).

The power to organize resistance and transform society pivots around our
collective ability to tell an honest story. In the context of capitalist
control, this will require a touch of magic. As such, The Honest Sorcerer has
chosen an apt name.

We leave Port Orchard gazing at smoky skies and arrive in Boston beneath
clouds of soot. My grandson will be roughly my age when this century runs out.
There is no reason to suspect that the climate will not heat to the point of
mass extinction by that iconic turn of the century. There are gathering voices
like those of Jeremy Lent and Balázs Matics that will inspire people, or not.
As grandparents, we are obliged to help tell the needed, truthful story.
